sections.h2: Colorado tax on house sale profit
sections.html:
No standalone capital gains tax exists in Colorado. Profit on a house lands in ordinary income, since the state begins with your federal taxable income and applies its own additions and subtractions. The state's Individual Income Tax Guide lays out that starting point.

One rate applies. C.R.S. 39-22-104 imposes 4.40 percent on federal taxable income for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2022, subject to the exceptions it names. Check the current Colorado return booklet for the rate in the year you sell, since the statute refers to other provisions that can change the rate actually charged.

Work out the federal result first, then layer Colorado's adjustments on top. If your federal return shows no taxable gain on the house, Colorado normally shows none either.

A typical owner-occupant pays no tax on profit up to $250,000, or $500,000 when spouses file together. The IRS explains the rule in Topic 701, and Colorado inherits the result.

Two tests look back over the five years that end on closing day:

  • Ownership: the house was yours for at least 24 months.
  • Use: it was your residence for at least 24 months.
  • The two stretches can fall on different months.

With a joint return, one spouse can satisfy ownership, but each must satisfy use. Skip the exclusion if you already claimed one on another home in the prior two years. Service members, Foreign Service staff and intelligence personnel on extended duty can pause that five year window for up to 10 years.

You may still have to report. A Form 1099-S in your mailbox means the sale goes on the return even if every dollar of gain is excludable, and any gain you cannot exclude must be reported too.

sections.h2: Which Colorado sellers are most likely to owe tax?
sections.html:
The sellers with an actual bill are landlords, owners who moved away long ago, heirs who rent the house before selling and flippers. If the house was never your main home, the use test fails and the whole gain is taxable.

Seller situationFederal home sale exclusionColorado treatment
Lived in the house 24 of the last 60 monthsUp to $250,000 single, $500,000 jointFollows federal taxable income
Rented out for years, never your residenceFails the use testGain is Colorado taxable income
Nonresident selling Colorado houseSame federal testColorado source income; withholding at closing
Sale paid over several yearsExclusion still availableInstallment method reported federally

If the buyer pays part of the price in a later year, the installment method applies unless you elect out, and you can still use the exclusion.

sections.h2: Selling a Colorado house from out of state
sections.html:
Colorado taxes gain from real property located in the state even if you live elsewhere. The state's part-year resident and nonresident guidance treats income from Colorado real property, including capital gains and losses, as Colorado source income.

Expect withholding at the closing table. When a nonresident conveys Colorado real property, the title or settlement company usually keeps back two percent of the price of the seller's interest, or the seller's net proceeds if that is smaller, and remits it with form DR 1079.

  • Withholding is an advance payment, not the final bill.
  • Enter it on the Colorado return on the DR 1079 line rather than the W-2 line.
  • Any excess over the tax due can come back as a refund.
  • The credit for tax paid to another state is closed to nonresidents.

Form DR 1083 and its instructions cover the withholding in more detail. A seller who expects little or no gain should raise it with the title officer early.

sections.h2: Colorado subtractions that can reduce the gain
sections.html:
A few narrow subtractions exist, and only some involve real estate. One removes the slice of gain that arises because Colorado basis in a property is higher than federal basis. Another removes income Colorado taxed in an earlier year, so no dollar is taxed twice.

The only capital gain subtraction tied to a property type covers agricultural land, and only farmers who meet the acquisition and holding rules can use it. A town house or city lot is out.

Wildfire mitigation, such as clearing defensible space around structures, has its own subtraction. It reduces income for work you paid for and does not shrink the sale gain, yet it may matter if you spent money on mitigation before listing.

Start with the sale price, take away selling costs, then take away adjusted basis. Topic 703 describes basis as roughly your purchase price, plus improvements that add value, minus depreciation and casualty reimbursements.

  • Count a new roof, an addition or a finished basement.
  • Hold on to the closing statement from your purchase.
  • Subtract depreciation if the house was ever a rental.
  • An inherited house usually carries a different basis than the purchase price your parent paid. IRS Publication 551 covers gifts and inheritances.

Take a married couple filing jointly who lived there for 10 years. They can exclude up to $500,000. Profit below that line means no federal tax and none in Colorado. Profit above it is taxed, with the Colorado rate stacked on the federal one.

sections.h2: When you pay Colorado tax on the sale
sections.html:
Payment comes with your return, or earlier through estimated payments. Quarterly Colorado estimates are generally due once liability, after withholding and credits, passes $1,000.

The filing trigger mirrors the federal one: a federal filer, or anyone owing Colorado tax, files in Colorado. Nonresidents and part-year residents with Colorado source income file under the same test.

This page covers state income tax only. Run your own numbers past a tax preparer.

A short checklist keeps the tax side of a Colorado sale from surprising you at closing.

  • Count your months of ownership and of living in the house across the last five years.
  • Add up improvement costs and subtract any depreciation you took.
  • Decide whether the sale will be reported on a joint or single return.
  • If you live outside Colorado, ask the title company how it will handle withholding.
  • Set aside money for estimated payments if you expect a taxable gain.

Taxes on the profit are identical whether the buyer pays cash or finances. The federal and Colorado rules attach to the price you accept.

Timing and cost are where a cash deal differs. An as-is sale skips repair spending and months of carrying costs, and a quick close may keep you inside the two year windows you were counting on. Sitting close to the 24 month mark? Check with a tax professional before signing.

Before accepting an offer, collect your purchase closing statement, receipts for major improvements and any Form 1099-S you expect. A preparer needs them whether the sale closes in a week or a quarter.

faqs.q: Is there a Colorado capital gains tax on selling a house?
faqs.a: No separate capital gains tax exists. The gain is part of Colorado taxable income, which starts from federal taxable income, and the statute sets a 4.40 percent rate for tax years from 2022.

faqs.q: How much of my house sale gain can I exclude?
faqs.a: Up to $250,000 if single, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the home at least 24 months of the five years before the sale.

faqs.q: Do I pay Colorado tax if I live in another state?
faqs.a: Yes, on gain from Colorado real property. The closing agent generally withholds the lesser of 2 percent of the sales price or your net proceeds, and you reconcile on a Colorado return.

faqs.q: Do I report a house sale if the gain is excluded?
faqs.a: Yes if you receive Form 1099-S. You must report the sale even when the gain is fully excludable.

faqs.q: Does Colorado have a capital gain break for farmland?
faqs.a: A subtraction exists for agricultural land, limited to farmers who meet the acquisition and holding rules. It does not apply to ordinary houses.
